reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: The aortic arch passes to the right of the trachea and crosses the right main bronchus rather than the left.
Two principal patterns exist: right arch with mirror-image branching and right arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery.
Mirror-image branching carries a very high association with cyanotic congenital heart disease, particularly tetralogy of Fallot and truncus arteriosus.
A right arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery arising from a Kommerell diverticulum, combined with a left-sided ligamentum arteriosum, completes a vascular ring.
This ring-forming configuration is strongly linked to 22q11.2 deletion, so genetic testing and cardiac evaluation are warranted.
Many isolated right arches are asymptomatic and found incidentally, but a ring may cause stridor, dysphagia and recurrent respiratory infection.
CT or MR angiography delineates the branching pattern, the presence of a Kommerell diverticulum and any airway compression.
Symptomatic vascular rings are treated surgically by dividing the ligamentum and, when the diverticulum is large, addressing it directly.
reference.pathophysiology: A right aortic arch arises when the embryonic left arch regresses and the right fourth arch and right dorsal aorta persist, reversing the normal pattern. In mirror-image branching the regression occurs distal to the ductus, producing branching that mirrors normal anatomy and rarely forming a ring, but coexisting conotruncal cardiac malformations are common. When instead the left dorsal aorta regresses between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, the left subclavian arises aberrantly from the descending aorta via a Kommerell diverticulum and passes behind the oesophagus; together with a left-sided ligamentum arteriosum this encircles the trachea and oesophagus to form a loose vascular ring that may compress these structures.
additionalDifferentials: Aberrant right subclavian artery with a left aortic arch
Tetralogy of Fallot or truncus arteriosus (as associated conditions)
additionalInvestigations: CT angiography of the aortic arch and great vessels
Transthoracic echocardiography to detect associated intracardiac defects
Barium swallow demonstrating a posterior oesophageal indentation
22q11.2 deletion testing by FISH or microarray
Chest radiograph noting a right-sided arch and an absent left aortic knuckle
redFlags: Cyanosis or a murmur suggesting associated cyanotic heart disease
Progressive stridor or respiratory distress from ring compression
Dysphagia with feeding difficulty and failure to thrive
Aneurysmal enlargement of a Kommerell diverticulum
reference.prognosis: An isolated asymptomatic right aortic arch requires no treatment and has an excellent prognosis; when it forms a symptomatic ring or accompanies congenital heart disease, outcome depends on surgical relief of compression and repair of the underlying cardiac lesion.
pitfalls: Overlooking the strong association between mirror-image branching and cyanotic congenital heart disease.
Failing to test for 22q11.2 deletion when an aberrant subclavian and ring are present.
Missing an enlarging Kommerell diverticulum that may require resection.
Assuming any right arch forms a ring, or conversely that all are innocuous.
Achieving incomplete symptom relief if the Kommerell diverticulum or ligamentum is not adequately addressed.
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
management: Observe with reassurance when the arch is isolated and asymptomatic, as no treatment is required
Surgical division of the vascular ring, including division of the ligamentum arteriosum and resection of a Kommerell diverticulum, for symptomatic tracheo-oesophageal compression
Airway and swallowing assessment with management of stridor, dysphagia and recurrent respiratory infection
Echocardiography and repair of associated congenital heart disease such as tetralogy of Fallot and truncus arteriosus
Testing for 22q11.2 deletion with genetic counselling in ring-forming configurations
Coordinated paediatric cardiology, cardiothoracic surgery and otolaryngology input
Follow-up for residual airway symptoms after ring division
